title: Off-by-one in a pagination helper
diff:
- return items.slice(start, pageSize)
+ return items.slice(start, start + pageSize)
explanation: The end index was just `pageSize` instead of `start + pageSize`. Page 0 happened to work by coincidence (start is 0), but every later page sliced the wrong window — often returning nothing at all.

title: A debounce that never debounces
explanation: Without a stored timer id to clear, every call schedules a new timeout instead of resetting the existing one — so `fn` still fires once per call, just delayed. It throttles nothing.

title: A loop that forgets its own index
diff:
- for (var i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
+ for (let i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so every callback closes over the same `i` — by the time the timeouts fire, the loop has already finished and `i` is `names.length` for all of them. `let` gives each iteration its own binding.

title: Sorting scores the wrong way
explanation: Array#sort() without a comparator sorts lexicographically — as strings. `[10, 2, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 2]`, and reversing that doesn't fix the ordering, it just flips the wrong order.

title: Fire-and-forget inside a loop
explanation: Array#forEach doesn't await its callback's return value, so the async callbacks all fire in parallel and the log line runs before any of them finish — the async/await inside is effectively decorative.

title: A falsy index breaks the check
explanation: indexOf returns 0 for a match at the very first position, and `0` is falsy — so the one case this function most needs to handle (the value being first in the list) is the one it silently gets wrong.

title: A "copy" that isn't one
explanation: A spread only shallow-copies the top level — `copy.address` is still the exact same object as `user.address`, so mutating it mutates the original too. Nested objects need their own spread.

title: The retry that gives up too early
explanation: If `fetch` itself rejects (network error, DNS failure, aborted request) rather than resolving with a non-ok response, the whole function throws immediately on attempt one — the retry loop never gets a chance to run.
